Patient Vignette: Anna M.

Anna M., a 50-year-old jeweler, sits in the chair across from me with her hands folded tightly in her lap. She is a petite woman with silver-streaked hair pulled back into a neat bun, and she wears a simple silver band on her right ring finger—the only jewelry she now allows herself to wear. She tells me she has been single for the past six years, and that she prefers it that way. "I don't trust people the way I used to," she says, her voice soft but steady.

The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late October. Anna had closed her small shop, Anna’s Atelier, at her usual time—7:00 PM. The shop is in a quiet, historic district of the city, a block of brick buildings with cobblestone alleys between them. She had just locked the front door when a man came up behind her, pressed something hard into her back, and demanded she open the safe. She remembers the cold metal of the knife against her spine, the smell of cigarette smoke on his jacket, the way his voice cracked when he said her name. He knew her name.

She opened the safe. She gave him the loose stones, the custom engagement rings, the antique brooches her grandmother had left her. He took everything and then, before he left, he hit her across the face with the butt of the knife. She fell, hit her head on the edge of the display counter, and lost consciousness. She woke up in the hospital with a concussion, a fractured cheekbone, and a police officer asking questions she could not answer.

In the months that followed, Anna tried to go back to work. She reopened the shop after six weeks, but the first customer who walked in—a man in a dark jacket—made her heart pound so hard she thought she was having a heart attack. She excused herself to the back room and vomited into the sink. She now works only by appointment, and only with clients she already knows. She has stopped taking on new commissions. Her bench, where she used to spend hours setting stones and shaping metal, is now cluttered with half-finished pieces she cannot bring herself to touch.

She describes the nightmares as "the worst part." Every night, she dreams she is back in that alley, but in the dream she cannot move. She tries to run, but her feet are glued to the cobblestones. She tries to scream, but no sound comes out. She wakes up gasping, her sheets soaked with sweat, and then she cannot fall back asleep because she is afraid the dream will return. She sleeps with the lights on now, and she has moved her bed so it faces the door.

During the day, she is hypervigilant. She scans every room she enters for exits. She avoids the alley behind her shop entirely, even if it means taking a longer route to the bus stop. She flinches when someone touches her unexpectedly. A few weeks ago, a friend put a hand on her shoulder to get her attention at a café, and Anna screamed so loudly that the manager asked them to leave.

She has withdrawn from almost everyone. She used to have dinner with her sister every Sunday; now she cancels with excuses about being tired or having a headache. She has not been to a movie theater or a restaurant in over a year. Crowds feel dangerous. Quiet feels dangerous. Being alone feels dangerous, but being with people feels exhausting.

When I ask her what she thinks about when she is alone, she pauses for a long time. "I think about how I should have seen it coming," she says. "I think about how I should have fought back. I think about how I just stood there and let him take everything." She blames herself for not being stronger, for not screaming, for not running. She tells me she feels like a different person now—weaker, smaller, afraid of her own shadow. "I used to be someone who made beautiful things," she says. "Now I'm just someone who survived."
